newsitem.title: UK: Miniature gas turbine can power homes, cars.
newsitem.headline: Miniature gas turbine can power homes, cars.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The Turbo Genset company says its new power generator is so compact and powerful that one day every home will have one.
Twenty years ago the notion that many families would have their own powerful miniature computer would have been scoffed at.

Turbo Genset's chairman, Professor Colin Besant, says like the laptop computer, his little gas turbines could one day have a ubiquitous presence in the home. They would provide cheap, clean and efficient power.
But first the company must prove itself in tough business markets.
Besant and a group of engineers at London's Imperial College have designed this new miniature gas turbine that with the help of new materials can produce huge amounts of power.

Using new magnetic substances called Neodymium-Iron-Boron and Samarium Cobalt, the gas turbine can spin at up to 60,000 revolutions a minute. This allows small machines to produce huge amounts of power and from a unit which is only 10 percent of the weight of a conventional turbine.

"Getting things to run at these high speeds is not easy. We actually hold the magnets in place with carbon composites, otherwise they'd fly out. A conventional generator is very heavy indeed. We plan to bring it down to a little unit that you can hold in your hand," Besant said in an interview at his company's stand at the Farnborough air show.

Turbo Genset, which is quoted on the Alberta stock exchange, has a broom-cupboard of a stand on the fringes of one of the exhibition halls, dwarfed by the likes of General Electric Co of the U.S. and Rolls-Royce.

But Turbo Genset hopes to start winning orders at the expense of established engineering companies. It is seeking its first sales from military and civil authorities like hospitals which need to have flexible backup power. This is now provided by huge diesel or piston engine machines which are hard to transport and inefficient to use.
The generators will also be small enough to fit into cars, and Turbo Genset will start testing with BMW's Rover and France's Renault next year to measure its viability to power electric cars.
Eventually smaller machines will be tailored made for the home. This offers a huge leap forward in the efficient use of energy.

"You lose a lot of power taking it to the home, you will probably get energy conversion of about 85 percent efficiency with this as opposed to something like 30 percent from the utility to the home," says Besant, who is head of Imperial's Department of Mechanical Engineering.

"We think power generation will go very much like computers. In the past it was all main frames, then the minis came in and now we all have PCs on our desks on a network. We think the same thing will happen with power generation. Everybody will have their own power generation running off the gas."
Besant says that because the exhaust gases from the turbine are much hotter than conventional turbines, these can be used also to heat water or run air conditioning.
"It will come first of all to office blocks, factories, and then it will gradually come down in size like, we've seen with computers."
"Eventually we'll end up with little microunits of this in the home. They can run on a wide range of fuels - anything that'll burn - natural gas, kerosene, diesel, even exotic fuels."
